amendments.rule: Reordered or discontinuous target tokens may occupy one unit when they realize one source item. Do not absorb unrelated intervening words into that unit. **Where English repeats one source function word because its scope is distributed across coordinated or emphatically repeated phrases or clauses, every English occurrence belongs to that source morpheme's one possibly discontinuous unit.** `מִן` in `מִבּוֹא בְדָמִים וְהוֹשֵׁוַע` → *from bloodguiltiness, and from avenging* takes both occurrences of *from*, while the waw takes only *and*; `בִּי אֲנִי` → *upon me ... upon me* gives both occurrences of *upon* to the single preposition while the suffix and explicit pronoun take their respective *me*. The repeated English word is neither `added` nor reassigned to a neighboring source item merely to make the units contiguous. **And the repeated word need not be one the source writes.** Where another rule assigns a supplied English function word to a morpheme's unit — a preposition the English verb's valency needs to reach its own object under rule 44, or a word the ASV supplies for a bare nominal under rule 33 — and the ASV writes that same word again over an elliptical or gapped parallel member, the second occurrence belongs to that same morpheme's one possibly discontinuous unit on exactly the terms above, however much stands between. `תְּבַקְשֶׁנָּה כַכָּסֶף וְכַמַּטְמוֹנִים תַּחְפְּשֶׂנָּה` → *search* ***for*** *her as* ***for*** *hid treasures* gives both *for*s to the verb, since the second stands for the searching the comparative clause elides, while each comparative `כְּ` takes only the *as* written for it. Do not read such a repetition as a second English word for the preposition, the conjunction or the comparative particle it stands beside, which would give one morpheme a two-word rendering the ASV writes for it nowhere else; and do not mark it `added` under rule 30, since the morpheme that licensed the first occurrence licenses this one. Test by subtraction as elsewhere — drop the repeated word and ask whether what has gone is the reach of a rendering already placed in the clause, or a relation no morpheme there carries. **An explicit personal pronoun is read the same way where the ASV resumes it in a later clause of the same verse.** Where a following verbless clause writes no subject of its own and the ASV supplies the subject pronoun that an explicit `הוּא`, `הֵמָּה`, `אֲנִי` or the like standing earlier in the verse denotes, both occurrences belong to that pronoun's one discontinuous unit, exactly as rule 18 gives both pronouns of a twice-rendered suffix to the suffix and rule 20 gives both halves of an identifying formula to its one `הוּא`: `הֵמָּה סֹחֲרֵי יָדֵךְ ... בָּם סֹחֲרָיִךְ` → *they were the merchants of thy hand ... in these were* ***they*** *thy merchants* gives both *they*s to the one `הֵמָּה`, headed on the first. Such a pronoun is not `added`, and it does not join the predicate's unit: rule 20 hands the predicate the construction's copula and, in a presentative clause, its dummy *there*, and a referential pronoun is neither, so the clause's supplied *were* goes to the predicate while the pronoun goes to the morpheme that denotes it. This governs a clause with no subject of its own: where a finite verb stands in the resumed clause it takes the English subject pronoun under rule 17, which is a pronoun realizing that verb's own person and number. **And where the Hebrew stands the pronoun is not part of the condition.** Hebrew postposes an explicit subject pronoun after its predicate and that predicate's adjuncts, often before a coordinated second subject, while English writes a subject before its verb; where the ASV writes the pronoun in both places it has realized one written morpheme twice, and both occurrences are that pronoun's one discontinuous unit, headed on the first English occurrence: `וְהִנֵּה נִצָּב עַל־עֹלָתוֹ הוּא וְכָל־שָׂרֵי מוֹאָב` → *and lo* ***he*** *was standing by his burnt offering,* ***he*** *and all the princes of Moab* gives both *he*s to the one `הוּא`, while `נִצָּב` keeps the *was standing* rule 20 leaves it and the coordinated subject keeps its own English. So read whether one written pronoun is realized twice rather than which side of the resumption it stands on, and do not hand the first occurrence to the predicate to make the units contiguous: rule 17's permission reaches a pronoun realizing a finite verb's own person and number, and a participle or other predicate morpheme in a verbless clause takes only the copula. **And the morpheme that denotes the resumed subject need not be a pronoun.** Where a common noun or a proper name written in the verse is the referent the ASV resumes, every English realization of that referent belongs to the noun's one possibly discontinuous unit on exactly the terms above, headed on the first English occurrence: `עַל־אֱלוֹהַּ נוֹרָא הוֹד` → ***God*** *hath upon* ***him*** *terrible majesty* gives both *God* and *him* to the one `אֱלוֹהַּ`, and `שַׁדַּי לֹא־מְצָאנֻהוּ שַׂגִּיא־כֹּחַ` → *Touching* ***the Almighty****, we cannot find him out;* ***He*** *is excellent in power* gives the resuming *He* to `שַׁדַּי`, while `שַׂגִּיא` keeps the *is excellent* rule 20 leaves it. This is the preceding paragraphs' own reasoning read for the morpheme that is actually written — the pronoun goes to the morpheme that denotes it — since what licenses the English word is that the verse writes the referent, and not the part of speech the ASV first realized it by. Rule 17's ruling that a supplied lexical subject noun is `added` does not reach such a pronoun: that ruling governs an English noun answering to no morpheme at all, as `יָשְׁבוּ בָהֶּ` → *men shall dwell therein* is, and here a written nominal answers to it, so read whether the verse writes the referent before marking a supplied subject `added` or folding it into the predicate under rule 20. **But that nominal must stand earlier in the Hebrew verse than the clause whose subject the ASV supplies, and what it does where it stands is no part of the condition.** Resumption is the continuing of a referent the verse has already named, which is why the paragraphs above ask for a nominal standing earlier in the verse; so read the source order rather than the English, and read whether the nominal is there to be continued rather than what case or office it holds. A vocative, a fronted topic or any other detached noun standing before that clause is a nominal the pronoun resumes and takes the pronoun exactly as a written subject does: `אַל בָּנָי ... מַעֲבִרִים עַם־יְהוָה` → *Nay,* ***my sons*** *... **ye** make Jehovah's people to transgress* gives *ye* to `בֵּן`, headed on *sons* under this rule's closing sentence, which is also what rule 36 means in refusing to mark a vocative's supplied *ye* `added`. Where instead the verse's only mention of that referent stands after that clause and inside a clause of its own, nothing there is being continued: the supplied pronoun answers to no morpheme this clause reaches and is its own `added` unit under rule 20's closing sentence, whatever a neighbouring verse names, since rule 10 makes the verse the whole unit of work. `מֵקִים מֵעָפָר דָּל ... כִּי לַיהוָה מְצֻקֵי אֶרֶץ` → ***He*** *raiseth up the poor out of the dust ... For the pillars of the earth are Jehovah's* leaves that *He* `added`, the name being written only as the predicate possessor of a later causal clause, while `יְהוָה מֵמִית וּמְחַיֶּה מוֹרִיד שְׁאוֹל וַיָּעַל` → *Jehovah killeth, and maketh alive:* ***He*** *bringeth down to Sheol, and bringeth up* gives its *He* to the `יְהוָה` standing at the head of the verse, and 1SA.2.6 and 1SA.2.8 are the two shapes in one chapter. The cataphoric case below is the limit of this and not a counter-example: `בְּפֶה חָנֵף` writes its possessive before the lexeme-bearing word inside a clause the noun itself stands in, which is a reordering this rule allows, and not a reach forward into a clause the noun has nothing to do with. **But every sentence above places an English word for a clause that writes no morpheme of its own for it, and a supplied object filling a gap the Hebrew leaves is not one.** Hebrew coordinates a second verb without repeating the object English must write, and a pronoun the ASV supplies there is rule 44's: it answers to no morpheme in the clause it stands in, is its own `added` unit, and is not folded into the noun that names the referent, however plainly the verse names it earlier. `אֶת־בְּנֵיכֶם יִקָּח וְשָׂם לוֹ` → *he will take your sons, and appoint* ***them*** *unto him* and `וְאֶת־שְׂדוֹתֵיכֶם ... יִקָּח וְנָתַן לַעֲבָדָיו` → *he will take your fields ... and give* ***them*** *to his servants* both leave that *them* `added`. What the sentences above place is a pronoun supplied where a clause writes no subject of its own, or a second realization of one written phrase, and a noun the ASV has already rendered as the object of its own verb is not a home for a second English word, as rule 51 says of a waw. This does not touch the distributed reading above, which reaches an English word the ASV writes a second time over a gapped member — the second *of* of `יַעְשֹׂר` → *the tenth of your seed and of your vineyards* — while a pronoun written once, for an object the Hebrew writes in no member at all, repeats nothing. Test by subtraction as elsewhere: drop the pronoun and ask whether a morpheme standing in that clause has lost its rendering, or whether only the English verb has been left without the object its valency requires. Read whether the clause the pronoun stands in writes a morpheme for it, and not whether the verse names the thing; where a written object morpheme does stand there, rule 18 gives it the pronoun as before. **But the morpheme those sentences look for is one the verse writes as a nominal of its own, and a finite verb's inflection is not one.** Where the only morpheme in the verse denoting that referent is the person and number of a finite verb, rule 17 has already realized it as that verb's own subject pronoun, and a further subject pronoun the ASV supplies for a coordinated verbless clause answers to nothing left in the verse: it is its own `added` unit under rule 20's closing sentence, while the copula joins the predicate as that rule directs. `יִצְפֹּן לַיְשָׁרִים תּוּשִׁיָּה מָגֵן לְהֹלְכֵי תֹם` → ***He*** *layeth up sound wisdom for the upright;* ***He*** ***is*** *a shield to them that walk in integrity* gives the first *He* to `יִצְפֹּן` under rule 17, leaves the second `added`, and puts the *is* on `מָגֵן`. Read what the verse writes rather than what the passage is about, since a referent named in a neighbouring verse is not written in this one and rule 10 makes the verse the whole unit of work; where the verse does write the nominal, the preceding paragraph governs as before. **But a morpheme already holding a pronoun of its own is not a home for a second one.** Where more than one morpheme in the verse denotes that referent, each takes only the English written for it, as rule 51 says of a waw and rule 43 of a spent preposition: the object suffix of `מְצָאנֻהוּ` above takes the *him* of *find him out* under rule 18, and the further *He* goes to `שַׁדַּי`. Count the ASV's realizations against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s. **And where the two realizations are not of the same kind, the head goes to the one writing the noun's own lexeme, whichever of them stands first.** The direction to head on the first English occurrence settles a tie between realizations of one kind — two *he*s, two *from*s, or a noun and the pronoun resuming it in that order — and it is not a preference for the phrase's left edge. Where the ASV realizes one written nominal both by a pronoun and by the word that writes its lexeme, rule 24 governs and the head is the lexeme-bearing word, exactly as rule 18 heads a twice-written suffix on the pronoun that realizes it directly rather than on the generic noun beside it, and as rule 31 keeps a head off a word the ASV supplied. This reaches a construct chain whose *nomen rectum* the ASV promotes to the clause's English subject while writing the chain's own relation as a possessive on the head noun: `בְּפֶה חָנֵף יַשְׁחִת רֵעֵהוּ` → *With* ***his*** *mouth* ***the godless man*** *destroyeth his neighbor* gives both *his* and *the godless man* to the one `חָנֵף`, headed on *godless*, while `פֶּה` keeps its own *mouth*, and `וּבְהַוַּת בֹּגְדִים יִלָּכֵדוּ` → *But* ***the treacherous*** *shall be taken in* ***their own*** *iniquity* divides the same way, headed on *treacherous*. Such a possessive is not `added` under rule 18's closing sentence and the promoted subject is not `added` under rule 17: a morpheme in the phrase answers to each, which is the count the paragraph above runs. Read which English word writes the lexeme before reaching for the first occurrence, since Hebrew writes the possessor after its head noun while English writes the possessive before it, so the pronoun stands first as often as not. **But an expletive the ASV writes to fill a subject slot English cannot leave empty realizes no referent at all, whatever the verse writes.** Where the ASV extraposes a clausal subject the Hebrew writes — an infinitive phrase, or another clause the ASV renders in full further on — and puts an anticipatory *it* where that subject would stand, the pronoun denotes nothing the verse names and rule 20 governs it: it is its own `added` unit, while the predicate keeps the copula that rule gives it and the extraposed clause keeps its own English. `תוֹעֲבַת כְּסִילִים סוּר מֵרָע` → ***it*** *is an abomination to fools to depart from evil* leaves that *it* `added`, with *is an abomination* on the construct noun and *to depart* on the infinitive. What the sentences above place is a pronoun denoting a referent the verse names and the ASV has rendered by a word of its own, so read what the pronoun stands for before folding it into a written morpheme's unit: `וְעֵץ חַיִּים תַּאֲוָה בָאָה` → *when the desire cometh,* ***it*** *is a tree of life* gives its *it* to `תַּאֲוָה`, which the ASV has already written as *the desire*, and one chapter may write both shapes, as PRO.13.12 and PRO.13.19 do. **An interrogative particle or a negative whose scope covers coordinated clauses is read the same way.** Where the Hebrew writes `הֲ` or `לֹא` once in the first of two coordinated clauses and the ASV rewrites it at the head of the second, every occurrence belongs to that one morpheme's discontinuous unit, headed on the first: `הֲלוֹא מַחֲזֵה־שָׁוְא חֲזִיתֶם וּמִקְסַם כָזָב אֲמַרְתֶּם` → ***Have*** *ye* ***not*** *seen a false vision, and* ***have*** *ye* ***not*** *spoken a lying divination* gives both *have*s to the `הֲ` and both *not*s to the `לֹא`, while each verb keeps only its own subject pronoun and lexical verb. This is rule 55's reading of a subordinator the ASV rewrites over a coordinated clause, applied to the particle that governs one. The second occurrence is neither `added` under rule 30 nor folded into the second clause's verb under rule 17. **Where in that first clause the morpheme stands is no part of the condition, and neither is a repetition of the same English word.** What licenses the second occurrence is that the morpheme's scope reaches the second clause, so a negative predicating of a verbless clause governs a coordinated colon from the middle of the first as readily as from its head, and the ASV answers it with whatever word carries the negation where that colon opens — a *Nor* or a *neither* as readily as a second *not*. `שְׂאֵת פְּנֵי־רָשָׁע לֹא־טוֹב לְהַטּוֹת צַדִּיק בַּמִּשְׁפָּט` → *To respect the person of the wicked is* ***not*** *good,* ***Nor*** *to turn aside the righteous in judgment* gives both *not* and *Nor* to the one `לֹא`, headed on the first. Read the clause's scope rather than the morpheme's position, exactly as rule 51 reads a postposed *also*, and do not mark such a word `added` under rule 14's closing sentences because no conjunction stands in the second colon: what that count marks is a coordinator no morpheme answers to, and what distinguishes a *Nor* from a bare *and* is the negation the written negative is there to license, as rule 35 says in heading such a word on the negative. An ASV italic on such a word corroborates it and decides nothing, by rule 7. But read what is actually written before applying it: where the Hebrew gaps the morpheme in the second line and a waw stands there, and the ASV writes a single word carrying both the coordination and the negation, rule 35 governs and that word goes to the waw, as `לֹא עֲלִיתֶם ... וַתִּגְדְרוּ` → *Ye have not gone up ..., neither built up* leaves the *neither* to the waw alone; and where no conjunction morpheme stands in that colon at all, rule 35's fusion has no coordination to rest on and the distributed reading above governs.
amendments.why: This chapter analysed one and the same construction two ways — a coordinated verb whose object the Hebrew gaps, with the ASV supplying *them* — folding the pronoun into the earlier written object noun at 1SA.8.11 and marking it `added` at 1SA.8.12, 1SA.8.14 and 1SA.8.16. Rule 44 already marks a supplied object pronoun `added` where no object morpheme stands in the clause; what licensed the other reading was rule 25's own sentence that *every English realization of that referent belongs to the noun's one possibly discontinuous unit*, whose surrounding paragraphs speak of a supplied **subject** but whose wording reaches any pronoun. The amendment narrows that sentence where it stands, rather than leaving the over-broad wording in place and adding a cross-reference elsewhere. It also marks the boundary against this rule's own distributed-function-word clause, which does reach a gapped member — the second *of* of `יַעְשֹׂר` → *the tenth of your seed and of your vineyards* at 1SA.8.15 — because there the ASV rewrites a word already placed, while the supplied *them* repeats nothing. Nothing in the corpus precedent contradicts it: rule 44's text already commands the outcome, and the change only stops rule 25 from licensing its contrary.

conventions: The king's-manner speech coordinates a second verb whose object the Hebrew gaps, and the ASV supplies a *them* English requires: וְשָׂם לוֹ (8.11), וְלָשׂוּם (8.12), וְנָתַן לַעֲבָדָיו (8.14), וְעָשָׂה לִמְלַאכְתּוֹ (8.16). Every one of those pronouns is its own `added` unit under rule 44, whether or not the verse names the referent earlier: no object morpheme stands in the clause the pronoun stands in, and a noun already rendered as the object of its own verb (בְּנֵיכֶם, שְׂדוֹתֵיכֶם and the rest) does not take a second English word. Rule 25's resumption was considered and set aside for all four.

יַעְשֹׂר (8.15, 8.17) is rendered by the light verb *take the tenth*, one unit headed on *tenth* under rule 44, and the *of* the English needs to reach its bare object joins that unit rather than the object noun. At 8.15 the ASV writes that *of* a second time over the coordinated member (*of your seed and of your vineyards*); both occurrences belong to the verb's one discontinuous unit under rule 25's clause on a supplied function word rewritten over a gapped member.

Do not read such a repetition as a second English word for the preposition, the conjunction or the comparative particle it stands beside, which would give one morpheme a two-word rendering the ASV writes for it nowhere else; and do not mark it `added` under rule 30, since the morpheme that licensed the first occurrence licenses this one. amended.why: This chapter analysed one and the same construction two ways — a coordinated verb whose object the Hebrew gaps, with the ASV supplying *them* — folding the pronoun into the earlier written object noun at 1SA.8.11 and marking it `added` at 1SA.8.12, 1SA.8.14 and 1SA.8.16. Rule 44 already marks a supplied object pronoun `added` where no object morpheme stands in the clause; what licensed the other reading was rule 25's own sentence that *every English realization of that referent belongs to the noun's one possibly discontinuous unit*, whose surrounding paragraphs speak of a supplied **subject** but whose wording reaches any pronoun. The amendment narrows that sentence where it stands, rather than leaving the over-broad wording in place and adding a cross-reference elsewhere. It also marks the boundary against this rule's own distributed-function-word clause, which does reach a gapped member — the second *of* of `יַעְשֹׂר` → *the tenth of your seed and of your vineyards* at 1SA.8.15 — because there the ASV rewrites a word already placed, while the supplied *them* repeats nothing. Nothing in the corpus precedent contradicts it: rule 44's text already commands the outcome, and the change only stops rule 25 from licensing its contrary.

report: One real split, in the king's-manner speech. The same construction - a coordinated verb whose object the Hebrew gaps and for which the ASV supplies *them* - was analysed two ways: 1SA.8.11 folded *them* into בְּנֵי as a rule 25 resumption, while 1SA.8.12, 1SA.8.14 and 1SA.8.16 marked the identical supplied pronoun `added` under rule 44. Rule 44 governs a supplied object pronoun and marks it `added` where no object morpheme stands in its clause; rule 25's resumption places a pronoun supplied where a clause writes no subject of its own, or a second realization of one written phrase, and בְּנֵיכֶם is already rendered as the object of יִקָּח. 1SA.8.11 is patched to agree with the other three.

The candidate table holds no other split. הוּא, וְ, לְ, בְּ, הַ, כְּ, אֶל, מֶלֶךְ, עַם, שְׁמוּאֵל and יהוה all vary with what the ASV wrote or with what stands beside them in the source: a rectum's *of* against a bare noun, a dative לְ silenced by a bare English indirect object against a written *to* or *unto*, an article whose *the* a suffix or a demonstrative has taken. שָׁפַט at 8.1 (predicate object of שׂים) against 8.2 (participial predicate with the construction's copula), and שַׂר at 8.12 (one written *for* before the first coordinated member, the second bare), are both licensed by the source. עָשַׂר at 8.15 and 8.17 is one treatment written over different amounts of coordination.

BSB disagreements are the documented convention difference throughout - BSB attaches the article, the object marker, the paragogic *he* and the preposition to the host word, where this project aligns each morpheme on its own merits (rules 12, 16, 32, 40). None is a genuine error. The one lexical candidate is כִּי at 1SA.8.9, where אַךְ כִּי is rendered by a single *howbeit*: the verse gave the word to אַךְ and marked כִּי `unrepresented` under rule 14's count, and a rule 30 fusion of the pair headed on אַךְ was available. It occurs once, nothing else in the chapter turns on it, and I did not change an accepted edge to improve an aggregate.

Left standing and named rather than changed: 1SA.8.14's *of them* at t016-t017, read as part of the substantival adjective's supplied noun phrase (rules 31, 46) rather than as a resumption of the three coordinated objects - it occurs once, and the verse pass named the competing reading. 1SA.8.19's *we* on הָיָה, where rule 43 keeps the possessive *have* on the written verb and the frame's subject pronoun with it though the ASV's *we* does not match the verb's person; the alternative would give *we* to a suffix already holding its own *us*.

Both large-source-unit candidates check out: 1SA.8.6 unit 2 (רַע בְּעֵינֵי → *displeased*) is rule 40's own fusion, the governed noun keeping no English of its own, and 1SA.8.18 unit 8 (מִלִּפְנֵי → *because of*) is rule 30's compound preposition read as one rendering rather than one token.
